title: True North vs Magnetic North: Declination Guide
description: Understand the difference between true and magnetic north with True North vs Magnetic North — declination, compass correction and worked examples. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, in New York your compass needle points about 13° west of true north, while in Los Angeles it points about 12° east of it — same country, opposite corrections, which is why this page exists.
quick_answer: True North vs Magnetic North explains the angle between the north your map uses and the north your compass finds — the declination. Learn which way your local needle leans, how much, and how to correct a bearing, so compass and map courses stop disagreeing by hundreds of metres.
steps_intro: Two norths, one needle — here is the angle between them:

body.t: The classic use: convert map bearings to compass bearings (and back) with your local declination before the leg, not after the confusion. The
tool gives the figure for your exact point.
Adjustable compasses take the correction once and then agree with the map all trip. This page explains what number you are dialling in and why it differs by region.
Panels and dishes are aligned to true bearings; installers working from a compass reading without correction can miss by the full declination — over 15° in the Pacific Northwest.
Historic surveys ran on magnetic bearings of their day. Declination drift since then is part of why an 1890 bearing does not retrace cleanly with a modern needle.

examples.label: Example · Correcting a bearing in New York

body.t: Declination near New York is about 13°W. A map bearing of 90° (due east) needs a compass course of 90 + 13 = 103° — with west declination, add the angle to go from true to magnetic.

examples.label: Example · The cost of ignoring it

body.t: Walk a one-mile leg with a 13° error and you finish about 0.23 miles — roughly 1,200 feet — off to the side of your target (the offset is the leg length times the tangent of the error). Small angle, long walk, missed cabin.

popular_table.title: Approximate declination, mid-2020s (WMM2025 era)
popular_table.intro: Rounded values for orientation — use the declination tool or NOAA for a current figure at your point.
popular_table.note: Values drift every year as the magnetic pole wanders — currently a few tenths of a degree per decade in most of the US, faster in places. Any printed figure ages; check the year on it.

faq: GPS positions are computed against true (geographic) north references — coordinates and map bearings are true. Only the compass needle answers to magnetic north, which is why phone compasses apply a model-based correction.

The line of zero declination, where compass and true north agree. In the mid-2020s it runs through the US Midwest-Gulf region and drifts westward over time — Chicago sits just west of it, hence its small westerly value.

Typically 0.05–0.15° per year in populated latitudes — Olympia, Washington's published figure changes about 0.12° per year westward. Over a decade on a stored map, that is a degree or more of silent error.
Does declination matter for short walks?
Barely — over a few hundred yards, even 15° is a modest offset and landmarks rescue you. It matters as legs lengthen and visibility shrinks: fog, forest, open water, night.
Why does my phone compass disagree with my handheld?
Phones apply a magnetic-model correction to display true north; a baseplate compass shows raw magnetic. Set the phone to magnetic in its settings, or adjust the baseplate, and the two agree.

Map grids (UTM, national grids) tilt slightly against true north too — a third north, usually within a degree or two at mid-latitudes. Serious map work keeps all three straight; most walkers only ever meet two.
Did explorers really navigate without knowing this?
They learned it the empirical way — variation was charted from the 1700s (Halley's Atlantic chart of 1701 mapped it), and good navigators carried local values the way they carried tide tables.
Where is the magnetic north pole now?

In the Canadian Arctic, a few hundred kilometres from the geographic pole, drifting toward Siberia at roughly 30–50 km per year in recent decades (published estimates). That drift is the engine under every number on this page.
